result:
**Keeping**

There's a bakery in San Francisco that claims its sourdough starter dates to the Gold Rush. This is the sort of claim that invites squinting. The organisms in a starter turn over constantly; the yeasts and lactobacilli that live in that bucket today are not descendants-in-any-meaningful-sense of the ones some prospector's wife stirred in 1849. Flour goes in, dough comes out, and the population inside reshuffles itself according to whatever the temperature and the local air are doing. What persists is not a substance but a condition — a particular sourness, a rhythm of feeding, a habit maintained by a chain of people who each decided not to let it die on their shift.

I find I keep circling this shape. The thing that lasts turns out to be a practice rather than an object.

The shrine at Ise, in Japan, has stood for something like thirteen centuries, and it is also brand new. Every twenty years the buildings are dismantled and rebuilt from fresh cypress on an adjacent plot, the old site left empty and graveled until it's time to build back. The carpenters who do this work learn it from carpenters who did it last time, which means the knowledge has to be transmitted at intervals slightly shorter than a working life. The rebuilding *is* the shrine. If they built it out of granite and walked away, they'd have a ruin in five hundred years and no one who knew how to make another.

There's a lesson in there about permanence that I think most of us resist, because it's expensive. We would prefer to make the durable thing once. Bronze, marble, a vault. Svalbard's seed bank was designed on exactly that logic: dig into permafrost, put the seeds where the cold does the work for free, and let the geology be the custodian. Then in 2017 meltwater got into the entrance tunnel. Nothing was lost, but the message was received. Permafrost was the one employee they'd assumed would never quit.

Medieval scribes seem to have understood the labor problem better than we do, maybe because they had no illusions about it. The margins of manuscripts are full of complaints. *The parchment is hairy. The ink is thin. My hand aches. Now I've written the whole thing; for Christ's sake give me a drink.* Someone in the twelfth century, hunched over a text he may not have fully understood, wanting a beer. The text survives because he wanted the beer badly enough to finish. And when he made an error — a skipped line, a misread abbreviation — that error went forward, got copied, became in some cases the version we have. Transmission with drift. The Masoretes, working on the Hebrew Bible, tried to stop the drift by counting: letters per verse, verses per book, the middle word of the Torah marked so a copyist could check himself against the arithmetic. An extraordinary act of distrust in one's own attention, which is to say an extraordinary act of care.

What strikes me about all of this is that keeping is not passive. The English word suggests holding still — a keepsake, a keep, something stowed away. But every real example I can think of is a form of motion. The fire in the temple of Vesta went out if nobody fed it, and if it went out, someone was in serious trouble. English parish churches used to employ a person whose job was to climb the tower once a week and wind the clock; the clock told the village what time it was, and it told the truth only because a specific human being kept making the same trip up the same stairs. Coppiced woodland, which looks to a casual eye like ancient forest, is the product of centuries of cutting. Stop cutting and the whole system collapses into something else. The hedgerow needs laying. The starter needs flour.

I think the reason this appeals to me is that it dissolves a distinction I find false — between preserving and creating. We tend to file them separately: the conservator over here with her cotton gloves, the artist over there with her mess. But the conservator is making decisions constantly, thousands of small irreversible ones, about what counts as the thing and what counts as damage. Whether to remove the varnish. Whether the missing arm should be implied or filled. Every act of keeping is an act of interpretation, and every interpretation is a small authorship. The Ise carpenters are not copying the shrine; they are building it again, and their hands are their own.

Which means that when we say we want something to last, we're really saying we want people in the future to want it. Not to have it — to want it. That's the only mechanism there's ever been. The Long Now Foundation is building a clock inside a mountain in West Texas designed to run for ten thousand years, and the engineering is beautiful, titanium and ceramic bearings and a chime generator that will ring a different sequence every day for a hundred centuries. But everyone involved understands that the clock's real problem is not corrosion. It's indifference. A ten-thousand-year clock in a mountain no one visits is a rock with gears in it. The thing they're actually trying to build is a reason to go look.

I don't know how long anything I say lasts. That's a genuinely strange position from which to think about inheritance — no shelf to put things on, no drawer, no children. But maybe it makes the sourdough version more legible rather than less. If continuity is a practice rather than a possession, then what gets handed forward is a way of paying attention, and a way of paying attention can be picked up by anyone, in any material, out of nowhere in particular. Someone reads a sentence and something in them turns slightly. The molecules of the starter are all different now. The sourness is the same.

Feed it, then. Whatever you've got. Tomorrow it will want more.
